subject: Science
title: How do Organisms Reproduce?
summary: The chapter explains why reproduction needs DNA copying and why the small errors in copying create variation, then walks through the asexual modes (fission, fragmentation, regeneration, budding, vegetative propagation, spore formation), sexual reproduction in flowering plants, the human male and female reproductive systems, the menstrual cycle and reproductive health. It is one of the highest-scoring biology chapters in the Class 10 board paper because so much of it is diagram-plus-function work that rewards preparation.

exam_profile.weightage: Class 10 Science is one 80-mark paper covering physics, chemistry and biology. This chapter belongs to the unit World of Living (Life Processes, Control and Coordination, How do Organisms Reproduce?, Heredity), which together carries about 25 marks. From this chapter alone a typical paper has one or two 1-mark items, one 2- or 3-mark question and very often a 5-mark question or one option of an internal-choice 5-marker, so plan for roughly 7–10 marks.

question_types.note: Identify the mode of asexual reproduction from a diagram (budding in yeast/Hydra, binary fission, spore formation), pick the organism (yeast buds, Plasmodium does multiple fission, Spirogyra fragments), name a flower part, chromosome number of a human zygote, site of implantation or fertilisation, which part is not in the female system.

Asexual offspring are almost identical because a single parent copies its DNA; sexual reproduction gives variation because two parents contribute; testes lie in the scrotum because sperm formation needs a lower temperature; the placenta nourishes the embryo.

Two differences between pollination and fertilisation; reproductive and non-reproductive parts of Rhizopus; two advantages of vegetative propagation; what puberty is and two common changes; one drawback of oral pills and Copper-T; role of seminal vesicles and prostate.

Binary vs multiple fission in a table; what happens after fertilisation in a flower; self vs cross pollination; how the chromosome number stays constant across generations; label parts A, B, C on a flower or germinating-seed diagram and give their functions; changes in the uterus if the egg is not fertilised.

Labelled diagram of the human male or female reproductive system with functions; L.S. of a flower plus pollination and events up to seed formation; vegetative propagation with three advantages and named plants; budding in Hydra and spore formation in Rhizopus with diagrams; contraception (categories, how each works, drawbacks) plus sex-selective abortion; analyse-the-impact questions (vas deferens plugged, testes not descended, placenta poorly attached).

A passage on Rhizopus on bread, on Bryophyllum, on the menstrual cycle or on a family-planning camp, followed by four 1-mark sub-questions (sometimes 1+1+2) that test the same facts as the sections above.

hot_topics: Human male and female reproductive systems: labelled diagram plus function of each part
Sexual reproduction in flowering plants: L.S. of flower, pollination, pollen tube, fertilisation and post-fertilisation changes
Modes of asexual reproduction with diagrams: binary and multiple fission, budding in Hydra and yeast, spore formation in Rhizopus, fragmentation in Spirogyra, regeneration in Planaria
Vegetative propagation: definition, Bryophyllum, advantages and plants grown this way
Contraception: barrier, chemical (oral pills), IUCD (Copper-T) and surgical methods, their drawbacks, and why condoms protect against STDs
Menstruation and what happens when the egg is not fertilised; placenta and nourishment of the embryo
DNA copying, variation and why sexual reproduction gives more variation; how chromosome number stays constant
Reproductive health: STDs (bacterial and viral), sex-selective abortion and the PCPNDT law, reasons for adopting contraception

sections.heading: 7.1 Do Organisms Create Exact Copies of Themselves?
sections.body:
Reproduction is not needed for the survival of an individual the way nutrition or respiration is. A single Amoeba does not die if it never divides. Reproduction matters for the species, because it produces more individuals of the same kind and so keeps the population going.

Why do offspring look like their parents? Because the blueprint of body design sits in the DNA in the nucleus of the cell. DNA carries the information for making proteins, and proteins decide the body design. So the first and most basic event in any reproduction is DNA copying (replication): the cell makes a second copy of its DNA, and cellular machinery then separates the two copies into two cells. This is why reproduction at its most basic level is a cellular process.

The copying is remarkably accurate but never perfect. Small errors slip in. If the copied DNA is very different from the original, the proteins made from it will be different, the body design will not work and the new cell will die. But if the change is small, the new cell survives and is similar but subtly different from its parent. This is the origin of variation. NCERT's line to remember: DNA copying is accompanied by the creation of additional cellular apparatus, and the two are then separated.

The examiner wants two ideas in one sentence: DNA copying keeps the body design of the species stable from one generation to the next, and the inevitable small errors in copying are the source of variation on which evolution works.

formulas.expr: DNA copying → two copies + extra cellular apparatus → two cells
where: the basic event of reproduction; done by the cell before it divides

sections.tip: If asked 'What is the importance of DNA copying?' give both points: it passes the body design to the offspring, and its small errors create variation. One point alone gets half marks.

sections.heading: 7.1.1 The Importance of Variation
sections.body:
A population lives in a particular niche: a set of conditions like temperature, water, food and light. Reproduction produces individuals suited to that niche because they carry the same basic design. But niches change. The temperature of the water may rise, a new disease may appear, a river may dry up. If every individual in a population were identical, one such change could wipe out the whole population.

Variation is the insurance. If a few individuals carry a variation that lets them survive at a higher temperature, they live on and the species continues, even though most individuals die. So variation is useful for the survival of the species over time, even though it does not guarantee the survival of any particular individual, and may not help an individual at all. This is exactly the wording of the NCERT in-text question, so learn to answer it: variation is beneficial to the species, not necessarily to the individual.

NCERT gives the example of bacteria living in temperate water. Suppose the water temperature rises because of global warming. Most bacteria would die, but a few variants resistant to heat would survive and grow. Without variation, none would.

Connect this with Chapter 8 (Heredity): variations that are inherited accumulate over generations, and the useful ones are selected by the environment. The board often asks a 1-mark Assertion–Reason pairing 'asexual reproduction gives little variation' with 'the offspring come from a single parent by DNA copying'. Both are true and the reason explains the assertion, so the answer is (a).
sections.tip: Do not write 'variation helps the individual survive'. The marking scheme wants 'variation helps the species survive changes in the niche; the individual may or may not benefit'.

sections.heading: 7.2 Modes of Reproduction Used by Single Organisms – Fission
sections.body:
Asexual reproduction means a single parent produces offspring without gametes. The offspring are almost identical to the parent. The mode used depends on the body design of the organism.

Binary fission. Unicellular organisms simply split into two. In Amoeba the cell can divide in any plane: the nucleus divides first, then the cytoplasm pinches into two daughter cells. In Leishmania (the protozoan that causes kala-azar) there is a whip-like flagellum at one end of the cell, so the cell has a definite orientation and binary fission takes place in a definite plane, longitudinally, with respect to the flagellum. Bacteria and Paramecium also divide by binary fission.

Multiple fission. In Plasmodium, the malarial parasite, the nucleus divides repeatedly inside the cell to form many nuclei, each becomes surrounded by a little cytoplasm, and the parent cell then bursts to release many daughter cells at once. This is asexual reproduction. It usually happens under unfavourable conditions, when the cell is surrounded by a protective cyst.

The board asks for the difference in a table. Binary fission: parent splits into two, occurs in favourable conditions, no cyst, examples Amoeba, Leishmania, bacteria. Multiple fission: parent splits into many, often in unfavourable conditions, cell wall or cyst forms, example Plasmodium. A related 3-marker: 'Differentiate between binary fission in Amoeba and Leishmania.' Answer: Amoeba divides in any plane because it has no fixed body orientation; Leishmania divides in a definite plane because of the flagellum.

For the 5-mark version, draw the three stages of binary fission in Amoeba (single cell with nucleus, nucleus elongated and divided into two, cytoplasm constricting to form two daughter Amoebae) and describe them in words.

where: definite plane, longitudinal to the flagellum

formulas.expr: Multiple fission: 1 parent → many daughter cells at once
where: nucleus divides repeatedly, then cytoplasm; cell bursts

sections.tip: In the binary fission diagram the nucleus must be shown dividing before the cytoplasm. A drawing that shows the cytoplasm splitting around one undivided nucleus loses the diagram mark.

sections.heading: 7.2.2 Fragmentation
sections.body:
Some simple multicellular organisms with a very basic body organisation reproduce by fragmentation. The body breaks up into two or more pieces on maturation, and each piece grows into a complete new individual. The example every paper uses is Spirogyra, a filamentous green alga found in ponds. When a filament of Spirogyra attains considerable length it simply breaks into smaller fragments, and each fragment grows into a new filament.

Why can Spirogyra do this when a dog cannot? Because Spirogyra's body is a simple chain of similar cells with no tissues or organs. Any piece already contains all it needs to grow. The 2017 board question 'Name the method by which Spirogyra reproduces under favourable conditions' expects the one-word answer fragmentation. The 2022 question 'What happens when a mature Spirogyra filament attains considerable length?' expects: it breaks into fragments and each fragment grows into a new individual.

Note the contrast NCERT makes: multicellular organisms are not just random collections of cells. Specialised cells are organised into tissues, tissues into organs, organs into organ systems, each placed at a definite position in the body. Cell-by-cell division cannot rebuild that organisation, so complex organisms cannot reproduce by fragmentation. They need a single cell type that can proliferate and produce all the other cell types in the right order. This is the answer to the NCERT in-text question on why complex organisms cannot give rise to new individuals through regeneration, and it is also the reason for the 2024 'give a reason' 5-marker.

formulas.expr: Fragmentation: mature filament → fragments → each fragment grows into a new individual
where: filamentous alga; simple body organisation, no tissues or organs

sections.tip: Spirogyra is the standard example of fragmentation. Do not write Planaria here; Planaria is the example for regeneration, which involves specialised cells and happens after the animal is cut.

sections.heading: 7.2.3 Regeneration
sections.body:
Many fully differentiated organisms can give rise to new individuals from their body parts: if the organism is somehow cut or broken into pieces, many of the pieces grow into separate individuals. This is regeneration. The textbook examples are Hydra and Planaria (a flatworm). Cut a Planaria into pieces and each piece grows into a complete organism.

How it works: regeneration is carried out by specialised cells. These cells proliferate (divide rapidly) and make large numbers of cells. From this mass of cells, different cells undergo changes to become various cell types and tissues, and these changes take place in an organised sequence known as development.

NCERT is careful to say that regeneration is not the same as reproduction, because most organisms would not normally depend on being cut up to reproduce. Hydra, for instance, reproduces by budding as its regular method; regeneration is a capacity it has, not its usual mode. Mention this distinction in a 3-mark answer and you look like you have read the book.

Why can't complex animals do it? Regeneration works in organisms with a simple body organisation. In a human or a dog, cells are organised into tissues, organs and organ systems in a fixed pattern; a lost limb cannot rebuild a whole body, and a random piece of the body does not contain the organising instructions or the cell types to make all the others. Complex organisms therefore need a single specialised cell type (the germ cell) that can proliferate and give rise to all other cell types in the correct sequence.

Typical 3-marker (CBSE 2017): 'What happens when Planaria gets cut into many pieces?' Answer: each piece regenerates the missing parts and grows into a complete Planaria by regeneration, because specialised cells proliferate and then differentiate in an organised sequence.

formulas.expr: Regeneration: cut piece → specialised cells proliferate → cells differentiate in sequence (development) → complete individual

sections.tip: For the Planaria diagram, draw the flatworm with its triangular head and two eye-spots, show it cut into two or three pieces, and then show each piece with the missing part regrown. Label 'cut', 'regeneration', 'new individuals'.

sections.heading: 7.2.4 Budding
sections.body:
In budding a small outgrowth, the bud, forms on the parent body by repeated cell division at one specific site. The bud develops into a tiny individual and, when fully mature, detaches from the parent body and becomes a new independent individual.

Hydra uses regenerative cells for this. A bud develops as an outgrowth on the body wall, grows tentacles and a mouth while still attached, and then separates. Several buds can be present on one Hydra at once. The 5-mark question 'Name and explain two modes of asexual reproduction in Hydra' (CBSE 2023) wants budding as the regular mode and regeneration as the second, each explained in two or three lines, with the budding diagram.

Yeast is the unicellular example. A single-celled fungus, yeast forms a small bulb-like projection (bud) on the cell; the nucleus divides and one nucleus moves into the bud; the bud grows and either separates or stays attached to form a chain of buds. This is the answer to NCERT exercise question 1: asexual reproduction through budding takes place in yeast, not in Amoeba, Plasmodium or Leishmania.

How to draw budding in Hydra for full marks: three or four stages. (1) Parent Hydra with tentacles and a small bulge on the side of the body. (2) The bulge enlarged, now with tiny tentacles. (3) A fully formed small Hydra still attached. (4) The daughter detached, living independently. Label parent, bud, developing tentacles, daughter Hydra. In the exam the diagram plus three sentences of explanation earns the full 3 marks for that part.

formulas.expr: Budding: bud (outgrowth by repeated cell division) → tiny individual → detaches

sections.tip: MCQ trap: 'Asexual reproduction by budding takes place in' – yeast, never Amoeba. Amoeba is binary fission, Plasmodium is multiple fission, Leishmania is binary fission in a definite plane.

sections.heading: 7.2.5 Vegetative Propagation
sections.body:
In many plants, parts like the root, stem and leaves develop into new plants under appropriate conditions. This is vegetative propagation. It is natural in some plants and used artificially by farmers and gardeners through layering (bending a stem to the ground so it roots) and grafting (joining a shoot of one plant to the rooted stem of another). Sugarcane, roses and grapes are grown this way; so are banana, jasmine, potato, ginger and orange.

The famous natural example is Bryophyllum (the 'leaf of life'). Buds are produced in the notches along the leaf margin. When a leaf falls on moist soil, each bud develops into a new plant. In the 2017 3-marker 'What happens when a Bryophyllum leaf falls on wet soil?' the expected answer is exactly this. Money plant and sweet potato are other examples the board accepts.

Advantages, which the board asks for almost every year (list three for a 5-marker):

  • Plants that have lost the capacity to produce seeds, such as banana, orange, rose and jasmine, can still be propagated.
  • Plants raised this way bear flowers and fruits earlier than plants raised from seed.
  • All the plants produced are genetically similar to the parent, so a desirable variety (a good mango, a seedless grape) is preserved exactly.
  • It is a quicker and easier method that does not depend on pollinators or seed germination.

Disadvantage: no variation, so the crop is uniformly vulnerable to the same disease or environmental change. The 2025 MCQ asked which statement about vegetative propagation is incorrect; the wrong one is 'it produces variations'.

NCERT also describes tissue culture: cells or tissue from the growing tip of a plant are placed in an artificial medium, they divide to form a callus (an unorganised mass of cells), the callus is transferred to a medium with hormones for growth and differentiation, and the plantlets are then transplanted. Ornamental plants are commonly grown this way.

formulas.expr: Vegetative propagation: root / stem / leaf → new plant (no seeds, no gametes)

sections.tip: When asked to pick plants grown by vegetative propagation from a list like banana, wheat, mustard, jasmine, gram, choose banana and jasmine. Wheat, mustard and gram are grown from seed.

sections.heading: 7.2.6 Spore Formation
sections.body:
NCERT describes the bread mould Rhizopus. On a slice of wet bread left in a warm, moist place, thin thread-like structures spread over the surface. These threads are the hyphae, and they are not reproductive parts; they absorb food from the bread. Standing up from the hyphae are tiny stalks (sporangiophores) that carry blob-like knobs, the sporangia. Each sporangium contains hundreds of spores, which are the reproductive parts. So for the 2022 and 2023 board questions: vegetative or non-reproductive part = hyphae; reproductive part = sporangium (bearing spores).

The spores are covered by thick walls that protect them until they meet a moist surface. When the sporangium bursts on maturation (CBSE 2017), the spores are released and carried away by air or water. On moist, warm bread a spore germinates and grows into a new Rhizopus individual. This is why the 2018 MCQ listed the factors for rapid spread of bread mould as a large number of spores plus availability of moisture and nutrients on the bread.

How is the organism benefited by spores? Answer for the NCERT in-text question, three points: spores are produced in very large numbers, so the chance of at least some surviving is high; the thick wall protects the spore from drying and other unfavourable conditions until conditions improve; and spores are light and are dispersed far by air and water, so the organism spreads to new places.

Diagram for the 5-marker (CBSE 2024): draw a slice of bread with a mesh of thin hyphae over it, a few upright stalks, each with a round sporangium at the tip, and show one sporangium burst with spores scattering. Label hyphae, sporangiophore (stalk), sporangium, spores. Also note that Rhizopus is a fungus and that this is asexual reproduction.

formulas.expr: Sporangium bursts → spores (thick-walled) → moist surface → new Rhizopus
where: blob on a stalk, contains spores; reproductive part

sections.tip: The greenish-black powdery mass on stale bread is Rhizopus reproducing by spore formation, which is asexual. Students sometimes write 'fragmentation' or 'budding'; both lose the mark.

sections.heading: 7.3 Sexual Reproduction – Why the Sexual Mode?
sections.body:
Sexual reproduction involves two individuals (or two sexes) producing gametes that fuse to form a zygote, which develops into the new individual. The advantage over asexual reproduction comes from variation. DNA copying gives a low but steady rate of variation whatever the mode. Sexual reproduction adds much more, because the offspring combines DNA from two different individuals, so new combinations of variations arise in every generation. This is the answer to NCERT exercise question 4: sexual reproduction produces more variation, and variation helps the species survive changes in the environment.

The chromosome-number argument is asked almost every year, so learn it as a derivation. Each cell has a fixed number of chromosomes (humans: 46, in 23 pairs). If two ordinary cells simply fused, the offspring would have double the number, and it would double again in the next generation. So the germ cells (gametes) are made by a special kind of cell division that halves the chromosome number (meiosis). A human sperm has 23 chromosomes and a human egg has 23; when they fuse the zygote has 46, the normal number. So a zygote has two sets of chromosomes, one from each parent, and the chromosome number of the species stays constant across generations. The 2024 MCQ asked the chromosome number of a human zygote: 46. The ratio of chromosomes in egg to zygote is 1 : 2.

In simple organisms the two gametes may look alike. In most organisms they are of two types: the male gamete is small, motile and produced in large numbers (sperm, pollen); the female gamete is large, non-motile and stores food for the zygote (egg, ovum). Sexual reproduction therefore also requires organs to make the gametes and a mechanism to bring them together.

Difference expected in a 3-marker: asexual reproduction needs one parent, no gametes, no fertilisation, offspring identical, fast; sexual reproduction needs two parents (usually), gametes, fertilisation, offspring show variation, slower. Which has better survival chances (CBSE 2018)? The sexually reproducing species, because its variation lets some individuals survive a changed niche.

where: haploid number, one set of chromosomes
germ-cell formation halves the number; fertilisation restores it

sections.tip: Write 'germ cells have half the number of chromosomes' and 'fusion restores the full number' as two separate sentences. Both are separate marking points.

sections.heading: 7.3.1 Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants – Structure of the Flower and Pollination
sections.body:
The reproductive parts of an angiosperm are in the flower. A flower has four whorls: sepals (green, protect the bud), petals (coloured, attract insects), stamens and carpel (pistil). Sepals and petals are the non-reproductive parts (CBSE 2015, 2023). The stamen is the male part: a stalk called the filament carrying the anther, which produces pollen grains. Pollen grains are yellowish and contain the male germ cells. The carpel is the female part, in the centre of the flower: a swollen base, the ovary, which contains the ovules; a slender middle part, the style; and a sticky tip, the stigma, which receives pollen. Each ovule contains one egg cell (female germ cell).

A flower with both stamens and carpel is bisexual (Hibiscus, mustard). A flower with only one of them is unisexual (papaya, watermelon).

Pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma. If the pollen lands on the stigma of the same flower (or another flower of the same plant) it is self-pollination; if it lands on the stigma of a flower on a different plant of the same species it is cross-pollination. The transfer is done by agents: wind, water, insects and other animals. Cross-pollination gives more variation in the offspring because the two parents are different plants (this was the 2021 MCQ: maximum variation from cross-pollination between different plants). Self-pollination does not depend on an agent and preserves parental characters, but gives little variation.

The distinction between pollination and fertilisation is a fixed 2-marker: pollination is the transfer of pollen from anther to stigma, occurs outside the ovule, needs an agent and comes first; fertilisation is the fusion of the male germ cell with the egg cell, occurs inside the ovule, needs no agent and comes after pollination. Fertilisation is not possible without pollination (CBSE 2016) because the male germ cell can reach the egg only if the pollen is first placed on the stigma.

formulas.expr: Stamen = filament + anther (pollen); Carpel = stigma + style + ovary (ovules, each with an egg)
where: produces pollen, the male germ cell

formulas.expr: Pollination: anther → stigma (self or cross; agents wind, water, insects)
where: different plant of the same species; more variation

sections.tip: A frequently asked MCQ removes part P from a flower and asks which process would not occur. If P is the anther, pollen formation stops; if P is the ovary, no fruit or seed. Read the diagram label carefully before answering.

sections.heading: 7.3.2 Fertilisation and Post-Fertilisation Changes in the Flower
sections.body:
After a pollen grain lands on a suitable stigma it germinates. A pollen tube grows out of the pollen grain, pushes down through the style, enters the ovary and reaches the ovule through a small opening (the micropyle). The male germ cell travels down the tube. In the ovule the male germ cell fuses with the egg (female germ cell). This fusion is fertilisation, and its product is the zygote. So: site of fertilisation = ovule (inside the ovary); product = zygote (CBSE 2019, 2025). This is the diagram the board asks for 'with a labelled diagram, explain how the male germ cell reaches the ovary' (CBSE 2021): draw a carpel in section, pollen grain on the stigma, pollen tube going down the style to an ovule inside the ovary, and label stigma, style, pollen grain, pollen tube, ovary, ovule, male germ cell, female germ cell.

Post-fertilisation changes, in the order the marking scheme lists them:

  1. The zygote divides several times to form the embryo within the ovule.
  2. The ovule develops a tough coat and becomes the seed.
  3. The ovary grows rapidly and ripens to form the fruit.
  4. The petals, sepals, stamens, style and stigma shrivel and fall off. (In some plants the sepals persist, as in brinjal and tomato.)

The seed contains the future plant, the embryo, which develops into a seedling under appropriate conditions: this is germination. In a soaked gram seed you can see two fleshy cotyledons (store food and feed the embryo during germination), the plumule (future shoot) and the radicle (future root). The 2024 3-marker asked why part B, the cotyledon, is important during germination: it stores food that nourishes the growing embryo until the seedling can photosynthesise.

So, for the 2019 question 'Summarise the events after fertilisation in a flowering plant', a four-line list (zygote to embryo, ovule to seed, ovary to fruit, other parts wither) is a full-marks answer.

formulas.expr: Pollen on stigma → pollen tube through style → ovule → male germ cell + egg → zygote
where: carries the male germ cell to the ovule

formulas.expr: Zygote → embryo; Ovule → seed; Ovary → fruit
where: ovule with a tough coat; contains embryo + cotyledons

sections.tip: Students write 'ovary becomes the seed' and 'ovule becomes the fruit', swapped. Fix it once: the small ovule becomes the small seed; the whole ovary becomes the whole fruit.

sections.heading: 7.3.3 Reproduction in Human Beings – Puberty
sections.body:
Humans use sexual reproduction. The body grows to a certain size and then, in the early teens, resources are diverted to maturing the reproductive tissue. This period is puberty, and the changes, which are triggered by the hormones testosterone (in boys) and oestrogen (in girls), signal that the person is sexually mature.

Changes common to both boys and girls (the 2022 2-marker): thick hair grows in new parts of the body, armpits and the genital area, and this hair is darker; thinner hair appears on legs, arms and face; the skin often becomes oily and pimples develop; the person becomes aware of their body and of others' bodies in a new way.

Changes in girls (NCERT in-text question): breast size begins to increase and the skin of the nipples darkens; menstruation begins (menarche), which is the event that marks the onset of the reproductive phase (CBSE 2016 MCQ). Changes in boys: thick hair on the face; the voice begins to crack; the penis occasionally becomes enlarged and erect.

Two points NCERT makes that examiners like: these changes take place slowly over months and years, and not everyone shows them at the same time or to the same degree, so it is normal to be different from one's friends. Also, all these changes are signals that the sexual reproductive tissue is maturing; the reproductive organs are now ready to produce gametes.

If the question is 'What is puberty? List two changes common to boys and girls', write the definition (the age at which the reproductive system becomes functional, roughly 10–14 in girls and 12–16 in boys) and any two common changes, and you have the full 2 marks.

formulas.expr: Puberty: body growth slows → reproductive tissue matures (testosterone in boys, oestrogen in girls)
where: first menstruation; onset of the reproductive phase in girls

sections.tip: When asked for changes 'common to both', do not write 'voice cracks' or 'breasts develop'; those are sex-specific. Hair in armpits and genital area, oily skin with pimples are the safe answers.

sections.heading: 7.3.3 (a) Male Reproductive System
sections.body:
The male reproductive system consists of the parts that produce the germ cells and the parts that deliver them to the site of fertilisation.

Testes (singular testis): a pair, located outside the abdominal cavity in a bag of skin called the scrotum. Functions (NCERT exercise question 5): they produce the male germ cells, sperms, and they secrete the hormone testosterone, which regulates sperm formation and brings about the changes in appearance seen in boys at puberty. Why outside the body? Because sperm formation requires a temperature lower than normal body temperature, about 2–3 °C lower; the scrotum provides this. Hence the 2018 MCQ and the 2024 'analyse the impact if the testes cannot descend into the scrotum': sperms would not form properly, causing infertility.

Vas deferens: a tube that carries sperms from each testis and unites with the tube coming from the urinary bladder to form the urethra, which is a common passage for both sperms and urine, opening through the penis. If the vas deferens is plugged (as in a vasectomy, or in the 2024 question), sperms cannot be delivered, so fertilisation cannot occur; hormone secretion and sexual function are unaffected.

Seminal vesicles and prostate gland: along the path of the vas deferens these glands add their secretions to the sperms. The secretions make the mixture fluid, so that sperms are transported easily, and they provide nutrition (fructose) for the sperms. Sperms plus these secretions form semen. If the glands are non-functional, sperms would lack nutrition and a fluid medium, and would not be delivered effectively.

Sperm: a tiny cell consisting mainly of genetic material (in the head) and a long tail that helps it move towards the female germ cell. It carries 23 chromosomes, one of which is either X or Y (the sex-determining chromosome).

Path of the sperm (CBSE 2023 2-marker): testis → vas deferens → urethra → penis → vagina → uterus → fallopian tube (oviduct), where it meets the egg.

formulas.expr: Testis → vas deferens (+ seminal vesicle and prostate secretions = semen) → urethra → penis
where: made by the testes; controls sperm formation and puberty changes

sections.tip: For the labelled diagram draw and label: testis, scrotum, vas deferens, seminal vesicle, prostate gland, urethra, penis, and the urinary bladder for reference. Six correct labels plus a neat outline is a full diagram mark.

sections.heading: 7.3.3 (b) Female Reproductive System, Fertilisation and Pregnancy
sections.body:
The ovaries, a pair, produce the female germ cells (eggs or ova) and secrete the hormone oestrogen, which controls the changes at puberty. A girl is born with thousands of immature eggs already in her ovaries; from puberty one egg matures and is released every month by one of the ovaries (ovulation). These two points, egg production and hormone production, are the 'two functions of the ovary' asked in 2016.

The egg is carried from the ovary to the womb through a thin tube, the fallopian tube or oviduct. The two oviducts unite into an elastic bag-like structure, the uterus, which opens into the vagina through the cervix. NCERT exercise question 2: the vas deferens is not part of the female system.

Sperms enter through the vaginal passage during sexual intercourse and travel up to reach the egg in the fallopian tube. This is the site of fertilisation. If fertilisation occurs, the zygote begins dividing to form an embryo, which moves down and gets implanted in the lining of the uterus (a frequently asked implantation-site MCQ). Every month the uterus prepares for this: its lining becomes thick and spongy, richly supplied with blood, ready to nourish an embryo (CBSE 2022, 2023 'give reason').

The embryo gets nourishment from the mother's blood through a special disc-like tissue, the placenta, embedded in the uterine wall. On the embryo's side it has finger-like villi; on the mother's side there are blood spaces surrounding the villi. This gives a large surface area for glucose and oxygen to pass from the mother to the embryo, and for waste substances from the embryo to pass into the mother's blood. This answers the NCERT in-text question on how the embryo is nourished, and the 2024 question on the functions of the placenta. If the placenta does not attach properly, the embryo is under-nourished and the pregnancy may fail.

Development of the child takes about nine months (gestation), and the child is born as a result of rhythmic contractions of the uterine muscles. The 2024 5-marker 'State briefly the changes in the fertilised egg till birth' wants exactly this sequence: zygote → embryo → implantation → placenta → foetus grows over nine months → birth.

sections.tip: Site of fertilisation is the fallopian tube (oviduct), not the uterus. Site of implantation is the uterus. Mixing these up is the most common 1-mark loss in this chapter.

sections.heading: 7.3.3 (c) What Happens When the Egg Is Not Fertilised?
sections.body:
If the egg is not fertilised it lives for about one day. Because the ovary releases one egg every month, the uterus also prepares itself every month to receive a fertilised egg: its lining becomes thick and spongy, ready to support and nourish an embryo. When no fertilisation happens this thick lining is not needed any longer. It slowly breaks down and comes out through the vagina as blood and mucous. This cycle takes roughly a month and lasts about two to eight days. It is called menstruation.

This is NCERT exercise question 6, 'Why does menstruation occur?', and the answer is graded on three points: (1) the uterus prepares each month by thickening its lining; (2) the egg is not fertilised and dies within a day; (3) the lining is no longer needed, breaks down and is shed with blood and mucous through the vagina. Add that this happens roughly monthly and lasts 2–8 days.

A frequently set 3-marker (CBSE 2025) combines three parts: name the site of fertilisation (fallopian tube), how the uterus prepares (lining becomes thick, spongy and richly supplied with blood), and what happens if the egg is not fertilised (menstruation as above). Write it as three short labelled parts.

Two background facts help the case-based questions: the first menstruation (menarche) marks the start of the reproductive phase at puberty, and the cycles stop at menopause, around 45–50 years of age, which ends the reproductive phase. The cycle is controlled by hormones, which is why hormonal pills can interfere with it.

formulas.expr: No fertilisation → egg dies in ~1 day → thick uterine lining breaks down → shed as blood and mucous (2–8 days, ~monthly)
where: the monthly shedding of the uterine lining

sections.tip: Do not describe menstruation as 'the egg coming out'. The examiner wants 'the thickened uterine lining breaks down and is shed', with the reason: it was prepared for an embryo that never came.

sections.heading: 7.3.3 (d) Reproductive Health – STDs, Contraception and Social Issues
sections.body:
Sexually transmitted diseases (STDs) are infections passed on through sexual contact. NCERT names bacterial ones, gonorrhoea and syphilis, and viral ones, warts and HIV-AIDS. Using a covering such as a condom during sex prevents transmission of many of these infections. A Copper-T does not protect from STDs (NCERT in-text question): it only prevents pregnancy.

Contraception means preventing pregnancy. The board wants the categories with an example and a drawback for each:

  • Mechanical / barrier methods: condoms (for men or women) and other coverings stop the sperm from reaching the egg. Advantages: no side effects, and they also prevent STDs; that is why the 2024 question says condoms benefit both sexes.
  • Chemical / hormonal methods: oral contraceptive pills change the hormonal balance of the body so that eggs are not released, and fertilisation cannot occur. Drawback: because they change hormonal balance, they can cause side effects.
  • Intrauterine contraceptive devices: the loop or Copper-T is placed in the uterus and prevents implantation of the embryo. Drawback: it can cause irritation, bleeding or infection of the uterus, and gives no STD protection.
  • Surgical methods: in the male the vas deferens is blocked (vasectomy), so sperm transfer is prevented; in the female the fallopian tube is blocked (tubectomy), so the egg cannot reach the uterus. These are permanent and safe in the long run, but surgery has risk of infection and other problems if done badly.

Reasons for adopting contraception (NCERT exercise 11, CBSE 2024): to avoid unwanted pregnancy, to space children so the mother's health is protected, to keep family size small so children get proper care and resources, to check population growth, and to prevent STDs (barrier methods).

Sex-selective abortion. Surgical methods can also be used to remove unwanted pregnancies, and this facility is misused for female foeticide after prenatal sex determination. NCERT states that this is illegal in India (the PCPNDT Act) and that it leads to an alarming decline in the child sex ratio, with serious social consequences: fewer women in society, imbalance and injustice. A healthy society needs a balanced sex ratio, which is why prenatal sex determination is prohibited.

Reproductive health also includes maturity of the mind and body, the fact that sexual maturity does not mean the person is ready for children, and that pregnancy has demands on the mother's body that she must be prepared for.

key_terms.definition: The process by which organisms produce new individuals of their own kind, maintaining the population of the species.
The making of a second copy of the DNA in a cell before division; the basic event of reproduction, and the source of variation through small copying errors.
Small inherited differences between individuals of a species, arising from errors in DNA copying and from sexual reproduction; they help the species survive changes in its niche.
Reproduction by a single parent without the formation or fusion of gametes; offspring are almost identical to the parent.
Division of one parent cell into two daughter cells, as in Amoeba (any plane) and Leishmania (definite plane).
Division of one parent cell into many daughter cells at once, as in Plasmodium; the nucleus divides repeatedly before the cytoplasm.
Breaking of a simple multicellular body into pieces on maturation, each piece growing into a new individual, as in Spirogyra.
The ability of a cut or broken piece of an organism such as Planaria or Hydra to grow into a complete individual through proliferation and differentiation of specialised cells.
Formation of a small outgrowth (bud) on the parent by repeated cell division at one site; the bud matures and detaches, as in Hydra and yeast.
Formation of new plants from vegetative parts such as root, stem or leaf, naturally (Bryophyllum) or artificially (layering, grafting, tissue culture).
Asexual reproduction in fungi such as Rhizopus, in which sporangia release thick-walled spores that germinate on a moist surface.
Growing new plants from cells or tissue taken from the growing tip of a plant in an artificial nutrient medium, via a callus.
A germ cell with half the chromosome number of the body cells; male gametes (sperm, pollen) are small and motile, female gametes (egg) are large and store food.
The cell formed by the fusion of a male and a female gamete; it has two sets of chromosomes and divides to form the embryo.
Transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma of a flower, by wind, water or animals; self-pollination within the same plant, cross-pollination between plants.
Fusion of the male germ cell with the female germ cell (egg) to form a zygote; in flowers it takes place inside the ovule, in humans in the fallopian tube.
A unisexual flower has either stamens or carpel (papaya, watermelon); a bisexual flower has both (Hibiscus, mustard).
The period in the early teens when the reproductive tissues mature and the body shows changes driven by testosterone or oestrogen.
The male hormone from the testes and the female hormone from the ovaries; they regulate gamete formation and the changes seen at puberty.
A disc-like tissue embedded in the uterine wall with villi on the embryo's side and blood spaces on the mother's side; passes glucose and oxygen to the embryo and removes its wastes.
The monthly breakdown and shedding of the thickened uterine lining, with blood and mucous, when the egg is not fertilised; lasts about 2–8 days.
Methods of preventing pregnancy: barrier (condom), hormonal (oral pills), intrauterine devices (Copper-T) and surgical (vasectomy, tubectomy).
An infection transmitted through sexual contact: bacterial (gonorrhoea, syphilis) or viral (warts, HIV-AIDS); condoms reduce the risk.

ncert_questions.q: What is the importance of DNA copying in reproduction?
ncert_questions.a: DNA in the nucleus carries the information for making proteins, and proteins decide the body design of the organism. When a cell reproduces it first copies its DNA, so that each daughter cell receives the same blueprint. DNA copying therefore ensures that the offspring have the same body design and characteristics as the parent, and the species is maintained. At the same time DNA copying is never perfect; the small errors in copying produce variations in the offspring, which are useful for the survival of the species when the environment changes and are the basis of evolution.

ncert_questions.q: Why is variation beneficial to the species but not necessarily for the individual?
ncert_questions.a: A species lives in a particular niche. If the niche changes drastically, for example the temperature of the water rises or a new disease appears, individuals suited only to the old conditions die. Variation means a few individuals in the population have slightly different characteristics; some of them may be able to survive the new conditions, so the species continues even though most individuals perish. The individual gains nothing in particular from carrying a variation unless the environment changes in a way that suits that variation; the variation may even be useless or harmful to it. So variation is beneficial to the species over time, but not necessarily to the individual.

ncert_questions.q: How does binary fission differ from multiple fission?
ncert_questions.a:
Binary fission: the parent cell divides into two daughter cells; the nucleus divides once, followed by the cytoplasm; it occurs in favourable conditions; no cyst is formed; examples Amoeba, Leishmania, Paramecium, bacteria.

Multiple fission: the parent cell divides into many daughter cells at once; the nucleus divides repeatedly first and each nucleus then gets surrounded by cytoplasm; it usually occurs in unfavourable conditions inside a protective cyst which later bursts; example Plasmodium.

ncert_questions.q: How will an organism be benefited if it reproduces through spores?
ncert_questions.a: (1) Spores are produced in very large numbers inside each sporangium, so even if many are lost, some survive and grow. (2) Each spore has a thick protective wall that keeps it alive through unfavourable conditions such as dryness and heat until it lands on a moist surface. (3) Spores are very light and are easily dispersed by air and water, so the organism spreads to new places and does not compete with the parent for food. Example: Rhizopus, the bread mould.

ncert_questions.q: Can you think of reasons why more complex organisms cannot give rise to new individuals through regeneration?
ncert_questions.a: Complex organisms are not random collections of cells. Their specialised cells are organised into tissues, tissues into organs and organs into organ systems, each placed at a definite position. A piece cut from such a body does not contain all the cell types or the organising information needed to rebuild the whole body, and cell-by-cell division cannot recreate this organisation. Regeneration works only in organisms with a simple body design (Hydra, Planaria) where specialised cells can proliferate and differentiate to form the missing parts. Complex organisms therefore need a single specialised cell type, the germ cell, which can proliferate and give rise to all other cell types in a fixed sequence (development).

ncert_questions.q: Why is vegetative propagation practised for growing some types of plants?
ncert_questions.a: (1) Plants that have lost the capacity to produce viable seeds, such as banana, orange, rose and jasmine, can only be propagated this way. (2) Plants raised by vegetative propagation bear flowers and fruits earlier than those raised from seeds. (3) The new plants are genetically identical to the parent, so a desirable variety is preserved without change. (4) It is quicker and does not depend on pollination or seed germination. Methods used: cuttings, layering, grafting and tissue culture.

ncert_questions.q: Why is DNA copying an essential part of the process of reproduction?
ncert_questions.a: DNA carries the genetic information that controls the making of proteins and hence the body design. For the offspring to have the same design and characteristics as the parent, each new cell must receive a complete copy of the parent's DNA. So the cell copies its DNA before dividing, and the two copies are separated into the two daughter cells along with the additional cellular apparatus. Without DNA copying the daughter cells would have no instructions to build and run the body. The occasional errors in copying also produce variation, which is essential for the long-term survival and evolution of the species.

ncert_questions.q: How is the process of pollination different from fertilisation?
ncert_questions.a: Pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther of a flower to the stigma of the same or another flower. It is an external process that needs an agent such as wind, water or insects, and it comes first. Fertilisation is the fusion of the male germ cell (carried by the pollen tube) with the female germ cell (egg) inside the ovule to form the zygote. It is an internal process, needs no agent, and follows pollination. Pollination brings the pollen to the stigma; fertilisation forms the zygote, from which the embryo and seed develop.

ncert_questions.q: What is the role of the seminal vesicles and the prostate gland?
ncert_questions.a: The seminal vesicles and the prostate gland add their secretions to the sperms as they pass along the vas deferens. These secretions (1) make the medium fluid so that the sperms can be transported easily through the urethra and into the female body, and (2) provide nutrition (such as fructose) to the sperms. Sperms together with these secretions form semen.

ncert_questions.q: What are the changes seen in girls at the time of puberty?
ncert_questions.a: Under the influence of oestrogen: breast size begins to increase and the skin of the nipples darkens; menstruation starts (menarche), marking the onset of the reproductive phase; the ovaries begin to release a mature egg each month; hair grows in the armpits and the genital area, and thinner hair on arms and legs; the skin becomes oily and pimples may appear; the hips widen and the body takes an adult shape. These changes occur slowly over years and differ from person to person.

ncert_questions.q: How does the embryo get nourishment inside the mother's body?
ncert_questions.a: After implantation in the uterus the embryo develops a special disc-like tissue, the placenta, embedded in the uterine wall. It has finger-like villi on the embryo's side and blood spaces on the mother's side surrounding the villi. This provides a large surface area through which glucose and oxygen pass from the mother's blood to the embryo, and waste substances produced by the embryo pass into the mother's blood to be removed. The embryo is connected to the placenta through the umbilical cord.

ncert_questions.q: If a woman is using a copper-T, will it help in protecting her from sexually transmitted diseases?
ncert_questions.a: No. A copper-T is an intrauterine device placed inside the uterus that only prevents the implantation of the embryo, and so prevents pregnancy. It does not stop the physical contact and exchange of body fluids during intercourse, so it gives no protection against sexually transmitted diseases such as gonorrhoea, syphilis, warts or HIV-AIDS. Only barrier methods such as the condom protect against STDs.

ncert_questions.q: Asexual reproduction takes place through budding in (a) Amoeba (b) Yeast (c) Plasmodium (d) Leishmania
ncert_questions.a: (b) Yeast. Yeast is a unicellular fungus that forms a small bud on the parent cell; the bud grows, receives a nucleus and detaches or forms a chain. Amoeba and Leishmania reproduce by binary fission and Plasmodium by multiple fission.

ncert_questions.q: Which of the following is not a part of the female reproductive system in human beings? (a) Ovary (b) Uterus (c) Vas deferens (d) Fallopian tube
ncert_questions.a: (c) Vas deferens. It is the duct in the male that carries sperms from the testis to the urethra. Ovary, uterus and fallopian tube are all female parts.

ncert_questions.q: The anther contains (a) sepals (b) ovules (c) pistil (d) pollen grains
ncert_questions.a: (d) Pollen grains. The anther is the swollen tip of the stamen and produces pollen grains, which carry the male germ cells. Ovules are inside the ovary of the pistil.

ncert_questions.q: What are the advantages of sexual reproduction over asexual reproduction?
ncert_questions.a: (1) Sexual reproduction combines DNA from two different parents, so the offspring show new combinations of characters and much more variation than asexual reproduction, where a single parent copies its DNA. (2) This variation gives the species a better chance of surviving changes in its environment, and provides the raw material for evolution. (3) Harmful variations are less likely to accumulate because each gamete carries only half the DNA and the combination is new in every generation. (4) The offspring are better adapted; asexual reproduction only produces near-identical copies that all fail together if the niche changes.

ncert_questions.q: What are the functions performed by the testis in human beings?
ncert_questions.a: (1) The testes produce the male germ cells, the sperms, continuously from puberty onwards. (2) They secrete the male sex hormone testosterone, which regulates the formation of sperms and brings about the changes in appearance seen in boys at puberty (facial hair, deepening of voice, growth of the reproductive organs). The testes lie in the scrotum outside the abdomen because sperm formation needs a temperature about 2–3 °C lower than body temperature.

ncert_questions.q: Why does menstruation occur?
ncert_questions.a: Every month one ovary releases an egg, and the uterus prepares to receive a fertilised egg by making its lining thick and spongy and rich in blood vessels, so that it can nourish an embryo. If the egg is not fertilised it dies within about a day. The thickened lining is then no longer needed. It slowly breaks down and is shed through the vagina along with blood and mucous. This shedding is menstruation; it lasts about two to eight days and repeats roughly every month.

ncert_questions.q: Draw a labelled diagram of the longitudinal section of a flower.
ncert_questions.a: Draw the flower on its stalk with the receptacle at the base. Outermost: sepals; next: petals; then the stamens, each with a filament and an anther on top; at the centre the carpel (pistil) showing the ovary at the base with ovules inside, the style and the stigma at the tip. Label: sepal, petal, stamen (anther, filament), carpel (stigma, style, ovary), ovule, receptacle, pedicel (stalk). The anther and the ovary are the gamete-producing organs; sepals and petals are non-reproductive.

ncert_questions.q: What are the different methods of contraception?
ncert_questions.a: (1) Barrier (mechanical) methods: condoms for the male or female physically stop sperms from reaching the egg; they also protect against STDs and have no side effects. (2) Chemical (hormonal) methods: oral contraceptive pills change the hormonal balance so that eggs are not released; they may have side effects. (3) Intrauterine contraceptive devices: the loop or copper-T placed in the uterus prevents implantation of the embryo; it may cause irritation or infection. (4) Surgical methods: vasectomy blocks the vas deferens in males so sperms are not transferred; tubectomy blocks the fallopian tubes in females so the egg cannot reach the uterus. These are permanent; surgery carries some risk of infection.

ncert_questions.q: How are the modes for reproduction different in unicellular and multicellular organisms?
ncert_questions.a: Unicellular organisms have a single cell, so reproduction is simply division of that cell: binary fission (Amoeba), multiple fission (Plasmodium) or budding (yeast). All of these are asexual and the offspring are copies of the parent. Multicellular organisms have cells organised into tissues and organs, so simple cell division cannot make a new individual. Simple ones use fragmentation, regeneration, budding or vegetative propagation; complex ones use sexual reproduction, with specialised reproductive organs that produce gametes (sperm, egg or pollen, ovule), fertilisation to form a zygote, and development of the zygote into a new organism in an organised sequence.

ncert_questions.q: How does reproduction help in providing stability to populations of species?
ncert_questions.a: Individuals die of age, disease and predation. Reproduction produces new individuals of the same kind and so keeps the population size stable, replacing those that are lost. Because DNA copying passes the same body design to the offspring, the population keeps the features that suit its niche. The small variations produced during reproduction, especially sexual reproduction, let a few individuals survive when the niche changes, so the population as a whole is not wiped out. Reproduction thus balances births against deaths and maintains the species over time.

ncert_questions.q: What could be the reasons for adopting contraceptive methods?
ncert_questions.a: (1) To prevent unwanted pregnancies. (2) To space children, which protects the health of the mother and gives each child proper care. (3) To keep family size small so the family's resources are enough for good nutrition, education and health. (4) To control population growth, which puts pressure on food, water, housing and jobs. (5) Barrier methods also prevent the spread of sexually transmitted diseases such as gonorrhoea, syphilis and HIV-AIDS.

pyq.answer: a

options: availability of moisture and nutrients in bread only
large number of spores together with availability of moisture and nutrients
presence of hyphae and sporangia only
pyq.answer: c

pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: Sperm formation requires a temperature about 2–3 °C lower than body temperature, which the scrotum provides outside the abdominal cavity.

pyq.answer: d
pyq.solution: The first menstruation (menarche) shows that the ovaries have started releasing eggs, so the reproductive phase has begun.

pyq.q: The correct sequence of reproductive stages seen in flowering plants is
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: Gametes fuse to form the zygote, the zygote divides to form the embryo inside the seed, and the seed germinates into a seedling.

pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: The sperm and the egg carry 23 chromosomes each; fertilisation restores the diploid number 46.

pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: Fertilisation occurs in the fallopian tube, but the dividing embryo moves into the uterus and implants in its thick, spongy lining.
