pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: Spirogyra breaks into fragments on maturity. Plasmodium does multiple fission, Leishmania binary fission, Rhizopus spore formation.

pyq.q: Which among the following is NOT a function of the testes at puberty?
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: The placenta forms in the uterus of a pregnant woman. The testes produce sperms and testosterone, which in turn regulates sperm formation.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Offspring produced by asexual reproduction show very little variation. Reason (R): In asexual reproduction a single parent copies its DNA and passes it to the offspring.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: With one parent and no gamete fusion, the only source of variation is the small errors in DNA copying, so the offspring are almost identical; R explains A.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): The testes in human males are located in the scrotum outside the abdominal cavity. Reason (R): Sperm formation requires a temperature lower than the normal body temperature.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: The scrotum keeps the testes about 2–3 °C cooler than the body, which is essential for sperm formation.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): The chromosome number of a species remains constant from one generation to the next in sexual reproduction. Reason (R): Gametes are formed by a special cell division that halves the chromosome number, and fertilisation restores it.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: Sperm (23) plus egg (23) gives a zygote with 46, the same as the parents; the halving during gamete formation is exactly why the number stays constant.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): A copper-T protects a woman from sexually transmitted diseases. Reason (R): A copper-T is placed in the uterus and prevents implantation of the embryo.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: d
pyq.solution: The reason is a correct statement of how a copper-T works, but preventing implantation does nothing to stop infection; only barrier methods protect from STDs, so A is false.

pyq.q: Rajesh observed a greenish-black powdery mass on a stale piece of bread. (a) Name the organism and the mode of asexual reproduction it shows. (b) Name its vegetative and reproductive parts.
pyq.answer:
(a) The organism is the bread mould Rhizopus, a fungus; it reproduces asexually by spore formation.

(b) Vegetative (non-reproductive) part: the thread-like hyphae, which spread over the bread and absorb food. Reproductive part: the sporangia, the round knobs on upright stalks, which contain the spores.

pyq.q: What is puberty? Mention any two changes common to both boys and girls in the early teenage years.
pyq.answer:
Puberty is the age in the early teens when the reproductive tissues mature under the action of testosterone or oestrogen and the body becomes capable of sexual reproduction.

Changes common to both: (1) thick, dark hair grows in the armpits and the genital area, with thinner hair on arms, legs and face; (2) the skin becomes oily and pimples appear. (Any two.)

pyq.q: (a) State one drawback each of the use of oral contraceptive pills and copper-T. (b) Under which category of contraception is the condom kept? How is it better than other methods?
pyq.answer:
(a) Oral pills change the hormonal balance of the body and can therefore cause side effects. A copper-T can cause irritation, bleeding or infection of the uterus and gives no protection against STDs.

(b) The condom is a barrier (mechanical) method. It is better because it has no side effects and, in addition to preventing pregnancy, it prevents the transmission of sexually transmitted diseases.

pyq.q: (a) Trace the path a male gamete takes to fertilise a female gamete after being released from the penis. (b) State the number of sets of chromosomes present in a zygote.
pyq.answer:
(a) Sperms are deposited in the vagina, swim up through the cervix into the uterus, and then into the fallopian tube (oviduct), where one sperm fuses with the egg.

(b) A zygote has two sets of chromosomes, one from the sperm and one from the egg (46 chromosomes in humans).

pyq.q: List any two contraceptive methods practised only by women. Mention how these methods work.
pyq.answer:
(1) Oral contraceptive pills: taken by the woman, they change the hormonal balance so that eggs are not released from the ovary and fertilisation cannot occur.

(2) Copper-T (intrauterine device): placed in the uterus, it prevents the implantation of the embryo. (Also acceptable: tubectomy, in which the fallopian tubes are blocked surgically so the egg cannot reach the uterus.)

pyq.q: In a flowering plant, summarise the events that take place after fertilisation.
pyq.answer: (1) The zygote divides repeatedly to form the embryo inside the ovule. (2) The ovule develops a tough coat and becomes the seed. (3) The ovary grows rapidly and ripens into the fruit. (4) The petals, sepals, stamens, style and stigma shrivel and fall off.

pyq.q: (a) Differentiate between binary fission in Amoeba and in Leishmania. (b) How does reproduction take place in the malarial parasite?
pyq.answer:
(a) In Amoeba the cell has no fixed shape or orientation, so binary fission can take place in any plane. In Leishmania there is a whip-like flagellum at one end, which gives the cell a definite orientation, so binary fission takes place in a definite plane, longitudinally with respect to the flagellum.

(b) The malarial parasite Plasmodium reproduces by multiple fission: the nucleus divides repeatedly into many nuclei, each nucleus is surrounded by a bit of cytoplasm, and the parent cell then bursts to release many daughter cells at once. This is asexual reproduction.

pyq.q: (a) Name the site of fertilisation in the human female. (b) How does the uterus prepare itself every month to receive the fertilised egg? (c) What happens if the egg is not fertilised?
pyq.answer:
(a) Fertilisation takes place in the fallopian tube (oviduct).

(b) Each month the lining of the uterus becomes thick and spongy and richly supplied with blood vessels, so that it can nourish the embryo after implantation.

(c) The unfertilised egg lives for about a day. The thickened lining is no longer needed, so it slowly breaks down and is shed through the vagina along with blood and mucous. This is menstruation; it lasts about 2–8 days and recurs roughly every month.

pyq.q: How do organisms, whether reproduced asexually or sexually, maintain a constant chromosome number through several generations? Explain with the help of a suitable example.
pyq.answer:
In asexual reproduction the parent cell copies its DNA and then divides, so each daughter cell receives exactly the same number of chromosomes as the parent; for example, an Amoeba divides by binary fission into two Amoebae with the same chromosome number.

In sexual reproduction two germ cells fuse. If they had the full chromosome number the offspring would have double the number, and this would double again every generation. So germ cells are formed by a special division that halves the chromosome number. In humans, body cells have 46 chromosomes; the sperm and the egg have 23 each; on fertilisation the zygote has 23 + 23 = 46, the same as the parents. In this way the chromosome number stays constant generation after generation.

pyq.q: In flowering plants pollen grains are transferred to the stigma by pollination, but the female germ cells are inside the ovary. Explain with the help of a labelled diagram how the male germ cell reaches the female germ cell.
pyq.answer:
After pollination the pollen grain on the stigma germinates and grows a pollen tube. The tube pushes down through the style, enters the ovary and reaches an ovule through the micropyle. The male germ cell travels down the pollen tube and fuses with the female germ cell (egg) inside the ovule, forming the zygote. This is fertilisation.

Diagram: carpel in section with stigma, style and ovary; a pollen grain on the stigma; a pollen tube running down through the style into the ovule; label pollen grain, pollen tube, stigma, style, ovary, ovule, male germ cell, female germ cell.

pyq.q: Differentiate between self-pollination and cross-pollination. Which of the two produces more variation in the offspring and why?
pyq.answer:
Self-pollination: pollen from the anther falls on the stigma of the same flower or another flower of the same plant; it does not need an external agent; the offspring are similar to the parent. Cross-pollination: pollen is carried from the anther of one plant to the stigma of a flower on a different plant of the same species; it needs an agent such as wind, water or insects; the offspring show new combinations of characters.

Cross-pollination produces more variation, because the male and female gametes come from two genetically different plants, so their DNA is combined in a new way in the zygote.

pyq.q: What is vegetative propagation? List with brief explanation three advantages of this practice. Select two plants from the following which are grown by this process: banana, wheat, mustard, jasmine, gram.
pyq.answer:
Vegetative propagation is a mode of asexual reproduction in plants in which new plants are produced from vegetative parts such as the root, stem or leaf, without seeds or gametes. It occurs naturally (Bryophyllum leaf buds, potato tubers) and is done artificially by cuttings, layering, grafting and tissue culture.

Advantages: (1) Seedless plants can be grown: plants that have lost the ability to produce viable seeds, such as banana, orange, rose and jasmine, can still be multiplied. (2) Earlier flowering and fruiting: plants raised vegetatively mature and bear flowers and fruits sooner than plants raised from seed. (3) Desirable characters are preserved: all the plants are genetically identical to the parent, so a good variety is maintained exactly. (Also: it is quicker and does not depend on pollinators or germination.)

Plants grown by vegetative propagation from the list: banana and jasmine. Wheat, mustard and gram are grown from seed.

pyq.q: (a) Describe the role of the prostate gland, the seminal vesicles and the testes in the human male reproductive system. (b) How is the surgical method of removing pregnancies misused in society? (c) Explain the role of oral pills in preventing conception.
pyq.answer:
(a) Testes: a pair of organs in the scrotum; they produce the male germ cells (sperms) and secrete testosterone, which regulates sperm formation and brings about the changes of puberty. They lie outside the abdomen because sperm formation needs a temperature 2–3 °C lower than body temperature. Seminal vesicles and prostate gland: they add their secretions to the sperms passing along the vas deferens; the secretions make the medium fluid so the sperms are transported easily, and provide nutrition to the sperms. Sperms plus secretions form semen.

(b) Surgical methods can remove unwanted pregnancies. This facility is misused for sex-selective abortion: the sex of the foetus is determined before birth and female foetuses are aborted (female foeticide). This is illegal in India and has led to a fall in the child sex ratio, which harms society.

(c) Oral contraceptive pills are taken by the woman and change the hormonal balance of the body so that a mature egg is not released from the ovary. With no egg, fertilisation cannot take place. Because they act on hormones they may cause side effects.

pyq.q: (a) Describe with the help of a diagram the various steps involved in binary fission. (b) Why do multicellular organisms need to use more complex ways of reproduction?
pyq.answer:
(a) Binary fission in Amoeba: (1) The Amoeba stops moving and its nucleus starts to elongate. (2) The nucleus divides into two, one for each half of the cell. (3) The cytoplasm constricts in the middle between the two nuclei. (4) The constriction deepens and the cell splits into two daughter Amoebae, each with one nucleus and identical DNA. Diagram: three stages, single cell with nucleus; cell with dividing nucleus; constricted cell and then two daughter cells; label nucleus, cytoplasm, constriction, daughter cells.

(b) Multicellular organisms are not random groups of cells. Their specialised cells are organised into tissues, tissues into organs and organs into organ systems, each in a definite position. A new organism cannot be produced by simple cell-by-cell division because that cannot recreate this organisation. They therefore need a single specialised cell type, the germ cell, that can proliferate and give rise to all the other cell types in an organised sequence (development), and organs to produce these germ cells and bring them together. This is why they use sexual reproduction with gametes, fertilisation and development.

pyq.q: Analyse the possible impact if in a human: (a) the testes cannot descend into the scrotum; (b) the vas deferens is plugged; (c) the prostate and seminal vesicles are non-functional; (d) the egg is not fertilised; (e) the placenta does not attach optimally to the uterus.
pyq.answer:
(a) Inside the abdomen the temperature is too high for sperm formation, which needs 2–3 °C less than body temperature; sperms are not formed properly and the man would be infertile (testosterone secretion may continue).

(b) Sperms formed in the testis cannot pass to the urethra, so they are not delivered; fertilisation cannot occur. This is the basis of vasectomy; hormone production and sexual function are unaffected.

(c) The secretions that make the semen fluid and nourish the sperms are absent; sperms would not be transported easily or get nutrition, so their ability to reach and fertilise the egg is greatly reduced.

(d) The egg dies within about a day; the thickened uterine lining is not needed, breaks down and is shed as menstruation; there is no pregnancy that month.

(e) The placenta is the only route for glucose and oxygen to reach the embryo and for wastes to leave. Poor attachment reduces this exchange, so the embryo is under-nourished, grows poorly and the pregnancy may fail.

pyq.q:
Read the passage and answer the questions. Bread left in a warm, damp cupboard for a few days develops a greenish-black, powdery growth. Under a hand lens, thin white threads are seen spreading over the surface, with tiny stalks standing up from them, each ending in a dark round knob. When a knob is touched it bursts and releases a fine dust that settles on nearby surfaces. In a few days the growth appears there too.
(i) Name the organism and the mode of reproduction described.
(ii) What are the thin white threads and the dark knobs called? Which of these is the reproductive part?
(iii) Why do the spores survive on dry surfaces and yet grow so quickly on the bread?
(iv) Give two ways in which reproducing by spores benefits the organism.
pyq.answer:
(i) The organism is Rhizopus (bread mould), a fungus, reproducing asexually by spore formation.

(ii) The threads are hyphae (vegetative, non-reproductive); the knobs are sporangia, which are the reproductive part because they contain the spores.

(iii) Each spore has a thick protective wall that keeps it alive through dryness; on bread there is moisture, warmth and nutrients, so the spore germinates and hyphae grow rapidly.

(iv) Spores are produced in very large numbers, so some always survive; they are light and dispersed by air to new places; the thick wall lets them wait out unfavourable conditions. (Any two.)

pyq.q:
Read the passage and answer the questions. In a health camp, a doctor explains to a group of young couples the different ways of avoiding pregnancy. She shows a condom, a strip of oral pills and a copper-T, and mentions that permanent surgical methods are also available. One participant asks whether the copper-T will also protect his wife from infections. Another asks why the doctor refuses to tell them the sex of an unborn child.
(i) Under which category of contraception does the condom fall, and what extra benefit does it give?
(ii) How do oral pills prevent pregnancy, and what is their drawback?
(iii) Answer the first participant's question with a reason.
(iv) Answer the second participant's question with a reason.
pyq.answer:
(i) The condom is a barrier (mechanical) method; besides preventing pregnancy it prevents the transmission of sexually transmitted diseases and has no side effects.

(ii) Oral pills change the hormonal balance so that eggs are not released, hence no fertilisation; because they alter hormones they can cause side effects.

(iii) No. A copper-T only prevents implantation of the embryo in the uterus; it does not stop the transfer of infection during intercourse, so it gives no protection against STDs such as gonorrhoea, syphilis or HIV-AIDS.

(iv) Prenatal sex determination is illegal in India because it is misused for female foeticide, which has lowered the child sex ratio and harms society; a healthy society needs a balanced sex ratio.

practice_mcq.q: Which of the following organisms reproduces by multiple fission?
practice_mcq.explanation: Plasmodium divides its nucleus many times and then splits into many daughter cells at once. Amoeba does binary fission, yeast and Hydra bud.

practice_mcq.q: Binary fission in Leishmania takes place in a definite plane because
options: it lives inside the human body
it has a whip-like flagellum at one end
practice_mcq.explanation: The flagellum gives the cell a fixed orientation, so it splits longitudinally with respect to it. Amoeba, with no fixed orientation, divides in any plane.

practice_mcq.q: The non-reproductive part of Rhizopus is the
practice_mcq.explanation: Hyphae are the thread-like vegetative structures that absorb food from the bread; sporangia and spores are reproductive.

practice_mcq.q: Buds along the notches of the leaf margin are used for vegetative propagation in
practice_mcq.explanation: Bryophyllum leaves carry buds in the notches; when a leaf falls on moist soil each bud grows into a plant. Potato uses tubers, sugarcane and rose use stem cuttings.

practice_mcq.q: Which statement about vegetative propagation is incorrect?
options: Plants that cannot produce seeds can be grown
The new plants bear flowers earlier
The offspring show a lot of variation
The offspring are genetically identical to the parent
practice_mcq.explanation: Vegetative propagation is asexual; the offspring are copies of the parent and show almost no variation.

practice_mcq.q: In a bisexual flower the parts not directly involved in reproduction are
practice_mcq.explanation: Sepals protect the bud and petals attract pollinators; stamens and carpel are the reproductive whorls.

practice_mcq.q: The male germ cell of a flowering plant is present in the
practice_mcq.explanation: Pollen grains produced by the anther contain the male germ cells; the ovule contains the female germ cell.

practice_mcq.q: After fertilisation in a flower, the ovary develops into the
practice_mcq.explanation: The ovary ripens into the fruit, the ovule becomes the seed and the zygote becomes the embryo.

practice_mcq.q: In a germinating gram seed, the future shoot and the future root are respectively the
practice_mcq.explanation: The plumule grows into the shoot and the radicle into the root; the cotyledons store food for the embryo.

practice_mcq.q: The number of chromosomes in a human sperm is
practice_mcq.explanation: Gametes carry half the diploid number: 23, one of which is the sex chromosome X or Y.

practice_mcq.q: Which hormone is secreted by the ovaries at puberty?
practice_mcq.explanation: Oestrogen from the ovaries brings about the changes seen in girls at puberty; testosterone is the testicular hormone.

practice_mcq.q: Fertilisation in the human female normally takes place in the
practice_mcq.explanation: The sperm meets the egg in the fallopian tube; the embryo then moves to the uterus for implantation.

practice_mcq.q: The common passage for urine and semen in the human male is the
practice_mcq.explanation: The vas deferens joins the tube from the urinary bladder to form the urethra, which carries both urine and sperms through the penis.

practice_mcq.q: Which of the following is a viral sexually transmitted disease according to NCERT?
practice_mcq.explanation: NCERT lists gonorrhoea and syphilis as bacterial STDs and warts and HIV-AIDS as viral ones. Typhoid is not an STD.

practice_mcq.q: Which contraceptive method works by preventing the implantation of the embryo?
practice_mcq.explanation: The copper-T sits in the uterus and prevents implantation. Condoms block sperm, pills stop egg release, vasectomy blocks the vas deferens.

practice_mcq.q: The unfertilised human egg survives for about
practice_mcq.explanation: If not fertilised, the egg lives about a day; the thickened uterine lining then breaks down and menstruation follows.

practice_mcq.q: Yeast and Hydra both reproduce by
practice_mcq.explanation: Both form a bud on the parent body that grows and detaches; yeast is unicellular and Hydra multicellular.

practice_mcq.q: Regeneration in Planaria is possible because
options: its specialised cells can proliferate and differentiate into all other cell types
practice_mcq.explanation: Planaria has a simple body organisation and specialised cells that multiply and then differentiate in an organised sequence to rebuild the missing parts.

practice_mcq.q: Which of the following gives the maximum variation in the offspring?
options: Cross-pollination between two different plants of the same species
practice_mcq.explanation: Only cross-pollination between different plants combines DNA from two genetically different parents; the other three give near-identical offspring.

practice_mcq.q: The placenta helps the embryo by
options: providing glucose and oxygen and removing wastes
practice_mcq.explanation: The villi of the placenta bathed in maternal blood give a large surface for glucose and oxygen to pass to the embryo and wastes to pass back.

common_mistakes: Writing 'the ovary becomes the seed and the ovule becomes the fruit'. It is the other way round: ovule → seed, ovary → fruit. Examiners deduct for each swapped pair.
Giving the uterus as the site of fertilisation. Fertilisation is in the fallopian tube; implantation is in the uterus.
Mixing up the organisms: yeast buds (not Amoeba), Plasmodium does multiple fission (not binary), Spirogyra fragments (not Planaria, which regenerates), Rhizopus makes spores (not buds).
Calling the hyphae of Rhizopus the reproductive part. Hyphae are vegetative; the sporangia with spores are reproductive.
Answering 'variation helps the individual survive'. The mark is for 'variation helps the species survive changes in its niche; the individual may not benefit'.
Listing sex-specific changes (voice cracking, breast growth) when asked for puberty changes common to both boys and girls. Use armpit and genital hair, oily skin and pimples.
Claiming that a copper-T or oral pills protect against STDs. Only barrier methods (condoms) do.
Drawing binary fission with the cytoplasm splitting around a single nucleus. The nucleus must divide first; the diagram mark depends on it.
Writing 'pollination = fertilisation' or describing pollination as fusion. Pollination is transfer of pollen to the stigma; fertilisation is fusion of gametes inside the ovule.
Forgetting the temperature reason for the scrotum. 'Testes lie outside the body' alone is a statement, not an explanation; add 'because sperm formation needs 2–3 °C lower than body temperature'.
strategy:
Divide the chapter into three blocks and give each one sitting. Block one is asexual reproduction: make a single table with organism, mode, one-line mechanism and the diagram thumbnail for Amoeba, Leishmania, Plasmodium, yeast, Hydra, Spirogyra, Planaria, Rhizopus and Bryophyllum. Practise the four diagrams (binary fission, budding in Hydra, spore formation, Planaria regeneration) until each takes under three minutes with labels. Add the vegetative propagation advantages as a fixed three-point list with named plants.

Block two is the flower: draw the L.S. of a flower and the pollen-tube diagram twice from memory, then write the two comparison tables (pollination vs fertilisation, self vs cross pollination) and the four post-fertilisation changes in order. These alone cover most 2- and 3-mark questions of the last five years.

Block three is human reproduction: draw the male and female systems and write one function against every label. Then learn the four contraception categories with one example, how it works and one drawback each, the NCERT names of the four STDs, and the reasons for contraception. Finish with the menstruation answer as three marking points and the placenta answer as structure plus two exchanges.

In the exam, take the 5-mark question from this chapter if there is an internal choice; it is almost always a diagram-plus-functions question that you have rehearsed. Spend about a minute per mark, draw with a pencil, label with a pen, and underline key terms such as fallopian tube, implantation and sporangium so the examiner spots the marking points.
